newsitem.title: USA: Clinton edges further ahead in Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Clinton edges further ahead in Reuters poll.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
President Bill Clinton climbed back towards a double digit lead over Republican Bob Dole in the Reuters daily tracking poll on Friday, stretching his advantage to 9.7 percentage points.

The poll, conducted by John Zogby Group International, tracks about 900 likely voters over a three-day period. The latest result, with a 3.3 percentage point margin of error, reflects polling taken Oct 8-10.
Clinton led Dole 43.8 percent to 34.1 percent. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot showed his first upward movement since the poll began, jumping to 8.7 percent. Some 12.3 percent remained undecided.
On Thursday, Clinton's lead was 8.5 points. Dole had narrowed the lead to only 5.3 points on Tuesday, following the first presidential debate last Sunday.
Daily tracking polls can show sharp fluctuations due to the relatively small sample of voters polled each day. Their chief value lies in tracking the trend over a period of several days.
By that measure, the campaign has not noticeably changed this week. Clinton began the week leading by 9.3 percentage points and ended it marginally better.

Since the poll began Oct 1, both candidates have fluctuated in a relatively narrow range. Clinton has never exceeded 50 percent or fallen below 43 percent. Dole has moved between a low of 30 percent and a high of 38.5 percent and is currently in the middle of that range.
Regionally, Clinton holds what appears to be an unassailable lead in the Northeast but all other regions of the country are competitive.

The two men are virtually tied in the South and Dole actually leads narrowly in the West, which includes the Rocky Mountain states. In the key Midwest-Great Lakes battleground, Clinton leads by seven points.

The president maintains his lead among all age groups, most noticeably among those aged 30 or less and those aged 65 or more. He leads in every income group except those earning $75,000 or more a year.
Clinton's lead is five points among men and 13 points among women.
The race for Congress remains a virtual dead heat and has hardly changed at all since the poll began.
